limitations: Unclear criteria used by human observers to categorize a patch in the image as a shadow.
Lack of understanding of mechanisms leading to the selection of particular constraints used by the visual system.
Unknown contribution of exposure to natural scenes to the final selection of constraints.
Unclear if attached shadows are processed in the occipito-temporal stream (shape) and cast shadows in the occipito-parietal stream (location).
Lack of knowledge about special neural mechanisms for measuring correlated motion between objects and their cast shadow.
Unclear how a visual system can compute spatial layout from cast shadow information (e.g., simple heuristics vs. cooperative estimates of scene properties).
Unclear how 'delocalized' shadow information is integrated with more local forms of depth information such as stereopsis.
The link between perceptual constraints and statistical properties of natural scenes remains to be ascertained.
minimum_safe_summary: This narrative review synthesizes research on the perception of cast shadows, concluding that they are weak cues for surface shape but highly salient for perceiving spatial arrangement and object motion in depth, especially when dynamic. The visual system resolves the inherent ambiguities of shadow motion by employing strong a priori constraints, such as assuming a stationary light source (typically from above) and a stationary background and viewpoint. Correlated motion between an object and its shadow is crucial for segmentation and linking. Limitations include an incomplete understanding of the neural mechanisms, the specific criteria used to categorize shadows, and how shadow information integrates with other depth cues.
